If the placenta is attached to the child by the umbilical cord, when will the placenta disintegrate?

The placenta is technically considered fetal-maternal circulation. When in the womb, their circulation is integrated.

After birth and taking its first few breaths, the child is no longer dependent on maternal circulation, and the cord can be cut without consequence.

Whether you cut the cord or not, the placenta has to be removed from the mother at this point, because it will actually begin degrading within the mother and can serve as a nidus of infection.

If the placenta is delivered and connected to the baby via the cord, the cord will ultimately disintegrate before the placenta does (because it is much smaller). Additionally, because it is no longer delivering blood to the baby, the cord itself really cannot stay alive for very long, so it will disintegrate.

As far as specific durations, I can't really say off of the top of my head. I believe the stump of the umbilical cord will fall off of the baby within a couple weeks, but at that point it is just a stump, it's not vascularized.

The placenta is not fed with blood from the child. Although it arises from the implantation of the embryo, it is partially derived from the uterine wall. It serves as an intermediary for the delivery of maternal blood to the fetus. So the placenta will being disintegration following delivery of the child.

When the child begins taking its first breaths, those vessels which were part of the maternal-fetal circulation close and disintegrate as the baby's lungs open up and fill with oxygen.
